extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students handling patent validity and infringement defenses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and pleading defenses to patent validity based on prior publication, prior patent specifications, prior use/sale, consent/acquiescence, and disclaimers; distinguishes experimental use and describes required notice and proof. Applicable in patent litigation evaluating anticipation, abandonment, and disclaimer issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign publication must fully enable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patented inventions cannot be superseded by ... a foreign publication ... unless the description and drawings contain and exhibit a substantial representation of the patented improvement, in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable any person, skilled in the art or science to which it appertains, to make, construct, and practise the invention to the same practical extent as they would be enabled to do if the information was derived from a prior patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere vague and general representations will not support the defence; the publication must enable those skilled in the art to understand nature and operation and to carry the invention into practical use. The account must be 'of a complete and operative invention capable of being put into practical operation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent/specification must disclose practicable mode
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior specification relied on to defeat novelty must not be merely a 'hint' — it must disclose a practicable mode of producing the result which is the effect of the subsequent discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House of Lords rule: an antecedent specification ought not to be held an anticipation unless it discloses a practicable mode; barren general descriptions or speculative suggestions cannot anticipate a specific, definite, practical invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior disclosure must equal patent's practical information
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The information as to the alleged invention, given by the prior publication, must, for the purpose of practical utility, be equal to that given by the subsequent patent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever is essential to the invention must be read out of the prior publication. If specific details are necessary for practical working and real utility, they must be substantially found in the prior publication. Apparent generality or overbroad propositions will not prejudice a later specific, limited disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of want of novelty: material part must be shown known
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant relying on prior knowledge or use must prove a material part of the invention was known or used before the patentee's discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior specification was broader than the patentee's real discovery due to wilful default or intent to defraud, the defence may succeed; if the overbreadth was accidental or inadvertent, the patent remains good for the bona fide, material, and substantial part of the invention, provided it is definitely distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and timing of disclaimer on novelty defence
rubrics_metrics.description: No costs can be recovered by a successful patentee in an action attacking novelty unless the patentee filed a disclaimer of the part wrongly claimed before bringing the action; unreasonable neglect or delay in entering a disclaimer may admit the defence of want of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclaimer is filed before action but its entry at the Patent Office was unreasonably delayed, the defence of want of novelty in any material respect will be admitted as a bar to the action; whether delay is unreasonable may be a question for the jury or the court depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must specify parts attacked in notice of defence
rubrics_metrics.description: When pleading statutory defences of prior use/knowledge, the defendant should first determine whether the whole or only part of the patented substance is open to objection and whether a disclaimer has been filed, and must specify in the notice of defence the particular parts intended to be attacked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defence that goes only to a part of the thing patented (leaving a material and substantial part unaffected) will not be a full answer to the action if a reasonable disclaimer has been filed; a defence that destroys the originality of the whole patent will be an answer regardless of disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirement vs evidence of state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires notice of matters relied on to defeat novelty, but it does not require notice for evidence merely showing the general state of the art at the time of the plaintiff's invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish evidence introduced to defeat the patentee's claim (requires notice) from explanatory evidence showing the state of the art (no notice required). Cases: evidence showing prior improvements in the field admitted without prior notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use/sale with consent/dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention had been in public use or on sale with the consent or allowance of the patentee before his application, this constitutes an abandonment or dedication to the public and defeats a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use includes making and selling the thing to be used by others or allowing it to be made by another with knowledge and without objection. If use was only experimental by the inventor, it is not 'public use.' The doctrine prevents an inventor from extending his exclusive period by delaying application after public adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge and acquiescence imply consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge by the inventor of public use or sale by others, coupled with silence or failure to assert exclusive rights, furnishes strong evidence (and in some cases conclusive proof) of acquiescence and therefore dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long acquiescence or very general use by the public is often conclusive. Whether knowledge is proved or may be presumed from circumstances can be a jury question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge may be presumed from circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct proof of the inventor's knowledge of public use is not always required; such knowledge may be presumed from the circumstances of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption of knowledge depends on facts and is often a question for the jury; the law treats circumstantial proof as sufficient where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed time required after knowledge for abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Once knowledge and acquiescence are established, no particular lapse of time is necessary to prove abandonment or dedication to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cites cases where many years of public use without assertion led to dedication; context and extent of use remain important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's intention is not decisive where public use exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The intention of the inventor is generally not the true ground; if he suffers the invention to get into public use without immediate assertion of his right, he is not entitled to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the knowledge was imparted fraudulently by another, the inventor must assert his rights promptly; otherwise his silence evidences acquiescence. However, intention does matter where the acts were purely experimental or for completion by the inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception for inventor's own practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use, exercise, or practice of the invention by the patentee himself for purposes of experiment or completion before applying for a patent does not constitute public use or dedication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary use as an accommodation or limited experiment, or use solely to try and perfect the invention, will not defeat the patent. The public use must be general or unlimited in time/extent/object to amount to dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication through third-party public use where inventor fails to act
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention becomes known to the public through third parties (fraudulently or otherwise) and the inventor knows of the public use and does not promptly assert rights, the inventor may be held to have acquiesced and thereby dedicated the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee should take immediate steps to legalize his rights upon notice; otherwise the public—who may be innocent users—are protected and the inventor may forfeit his claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for dedication when patentee used invention himself
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inventor practises his invention himself before applying, the general test is whether the use was for the purpose of gain (commercial/exploitative) rather than experimental; if evidence does not prove use for gain, public use is not proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the inventor's acts were experiments to perfect the invention or acts indicating surrender to the public (e.g., widespread manufacture/sale). Evidence that stops short of demonstrating use for gain will not establish dedication.
